issues.legal_issue: Adoption does not divest an adoptive parent of property already vested in that parent unless an admissible agreement provides otherwise.
material_facts: The property had belonged to the adoptive parent's husband, and after his death the property vested in her as an absolute owner under the Hindu Succession Act.
She adopted a child after the property had vested in her.
The unregistered adoption deed included a covenant purporting to give the adopted child an immediate right to the property and to prevent her from alienating it.
She later transferred the property by a registered sale deed.
issues.conclusion: The adoption itself did not deprive the adoptive mother of her vested property rights. Although the parties could agree otherwise, the unregistered property covenant could not be admitted in evidence; it therefore did not prevent her from transferring the property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 12, proviso (c), of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, adoption does not divest a person of an estate vested before the adoption. Section 13 permits an agreement to the contrary, but the relevant covenant here required registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908, and could not be admitted under Section 49 because it was unregistered. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: adoption_property_dispute and property_vested_before_adoption and not contrary_agreement_admissible

predicates.adoption_property_dispute: The dispute concerns the effect of an adoption on property held by the adoptive parent.
predicates.property_vested_before_adoption: The property had already vested in the adoptive parent before the adoption.
predicates.contrary_agreement_admissible: The parties made an agreement contrary to the adoptive parent's usual power to dispose of the property, and that agreement is admissible in evidence.

issues.definition: When a property dispute concerns an adoption and the property vested in the adoptive parent beforehand, the parent retains power to transfer it if no admissible contrary agreement exists.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered instrument may be admitted to prove an adoption but not to prove a clause that creates or extinguishes rights in immovable property and requires registration.
material_facts: The instrument recited the adoption and also contained a covenant purporting to give the adopted child an immediate right in the property and to divest the adoptive mother's rights.
The trial court admitted the instrument to prove the adoption, while the High Court relied on the property covenant to conclude that the mother could not transfer the property.
issues.conclusion: The instrument could be admitted as evidence of the adoption, but its unregistered property-rights covenant could not be admitted to establish an immediate transfer or extinguishment of property rights.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908, requires registration of an instrument that creates, assigns, limits, or extinguishes rights in immovable property. Under Section 49, an unregistered instrument requiring registration cannot be admitted to prove that property transaction. The court did not rely on any earlier cases.

predicates.evidence_admissibility_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether an instrument may be admitted as evidence for a particular purpose.
predicates.instrument_contains_immediate_property_r: The instrument contains a clause purporting to create an immediate right in immovable property or extinguish another person's rights in it.

issues.definition: In an evidentiary dispute, an unregistered instrument containing a clause that purports to create or extinguish immediate rights in immovable property cannot be used to prove that property-rights transaction.
